newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania denies Telefonica claims over GSM.
newsitem.headline: Romania denies Telefonica claims over GSM.

text.p: Romania's communcations ministry on Wednesday dismissed as groundless threats by Spain's Telefonica de Espana SA to sue the Romanian government in a bid to block a tender for two GSM licenses.
"It's their (Telefonica's) business if they want to take us to court. But they are wrong. We won't change our plans for the tender," ministry counsellor Ion Matei told Reuters.
A Telefonica source said on Tuesday its Romanian branch had been promised the right over digital mobile telephone service when it started analogue service in Bucharest in 1992.
The source said Telefonica plans to take legal action against the winners of the bid, scheduled for September 26, if the company failed to stop Bucharest from going ahead with the tender.

"Our intepretation of the contract with Telefonica is that it has no exclusive rights over mobile telephony in Romania," Matei said. "It makes no sense to award a GSM licence directly to a firm. Only a tender can create competition."

Telefonica Romania, a joint stock company, was formed in June 1992 by Telefonica International, Romania's state-owned telecommunications operator Romtelecom, and Radiocomunicatii SA, which runs the transmitter network. The Spanish partner has a 60 percent stake in the firm.
The company covers only Romania's biggest cities.

The September 26 tender requires firms to be able to cover at least 65 percent of Romania with a digital GSM system in the 900 Mhz waveband, to have solid operating experience and financial strength for the project estimated at $1.0 billion.
Three consortia have submitted bids so far and the ministry said 60 companies had purchased the tender documents.

"The contract with Telefonica says the company has the right to operate an analogue mobile telephony system on the 450 Mhz waveband. Or, our tender is for a digital system on the 900 Mhz waveband," Matei said, adding that under the contract Telefonica was only an operator, without mentioning any services required for the GSM system.

Matei said any initial promises made to Telefonica that it would have the right to offer digital mobile telephone services had been intended by the ministry to prevent the company from being excluded from future tenders.

"It was actually our wish to give Telefonica the right to take part in any tender and not to be excluded in an arbitrary way from getting a licence for digital mobile telephony simply because it already has one for an analogue system," he said. -- Adrian Dascalu, Bucharest Newsroom 40-1 3120264
